office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The 'Tipton Community School Board' seats belong to Tipton Community School Corporation (TCSC) in Tipton, Tipton County, which runs Tipton Elementary, Tipton Middle and Tipton High School [24, 25]. Federal data list 1,366 students in 2024-25, and the district says enrollment has declined gradually over the past decade [25, 26]. Scott Jaworski became superintendent on July 1, 2026, succeeding the retired Ryan Glaze; the board chose him in 2025 and he served as associate superintendent and then interim superintendent during the transition [27, 28, 29].

The board has seven members: Rob Cochrane (president), Jennifer Humrichous (vice president), Kimberly Fague (secretary), Tami Brown, Andrea Campbell, Eric Underwood and Beth Woelfert [30, 31]. Members are elected from residence areas that include the City of Tipton and Cicero Township; the district site does not describe the full seat plan [30, 32, 33].

Cicero Township: Robert Cochrane won this seat unopposed in 2022 and is running again, unopposed [34, 6]. Cicero Township has a second seat, filled by Beth Woelfert in the 2024 election, which is not on the 2026 ballot [33, 35].

City of Tipton — likely two seats, not one: in 2022 voters filled two City of Tipton seats, electing Jason Springer and Eric Underwood and unseating incumbent Chris McNew [32, 34]. Springer resigned in September 2024, and the board interviewed six people in November 2024 to serve the rest of his term; it appointed Tamera Brown and Kimberly Fague to fill vacancies in late 2024 [36, 35]. Both 2022 City seats would normally be up in 2026, but the state list shows this race as 'vote for 1'; this guide could not confirm the number of seats from an official 2026 ballot [6].

Incumbents running: Cochrane (Cicero Township) and Eric Underwood (City of Tipton) are current members on the ballot; Tamera Noble Brown appears to be the board member listed as Tami Brown, who was appointed in late 2024, though no fetched source gives her full name [6, 30, 35].
Party labels: the state list shows Cochrane, Underwood and Tamera Noble Brown with the Republican label, Caiden C. McNew as Democratic and Christopher K. McNew as Independent [6].

Operating referendum on the same ballot: on June 30, 2026 the board approved placing the district's first operating referendum on the November 3 ballot, asking for a tax rate of up to $0.25 per $100 of assessed value for up to eight years, raising no more than $2 million a year [37, 38]. The district estimates the cost for a median home at $174 to $216 a year and about $4 per acre of farmland, and says the money would go to academic programs, student supports, staff recruitment and retention, transportation and operations, not construction or athletic facilities [37, 38].

Budget and SEA 1: the district cites revenue losses from the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1), property-tax cap (circuit breaker) losses, rising costs and declining enrollment, and says earlier cuts — staff reductions through attrition, shared positions, deferred maintenance and transportation changes — cannot fully close the gap; it says cuts to staffing, programs, transportation and student services may follow if the referendum fails [26, 39, 38]. The district's pages do not give a dollar figure for the SEA 1 loss [26, 39].

Fees: in January 2026 the board approved transportation participation fees to offset SEA 1 costs, including a fixed fee for extracurricular activities and a field trip fee; in July 2026 it kept the transportation fee at $5 per student per round trip, to be reviewed in June 2027 [31, 40]. Meal prices rise for 2026-27 to meet a required weighted average [29].

Facilities: a Tipton Elementary playground replacement was funded in part by a $200,000 Tipton County Foundation grant; in January 2026 the board put off a $2.95 million microturbine energy project, saying the upfront cost was not feasible [31, 29].

Other 2026 actions: the board adopted 2026 legislative policy updates including wireless device restrictions (June 2026) and set a 2027 budget hearing for September 22 with adoption scheduled for October 13, 2026 [29, 40].

Forums: no 2026 candidate forum was found for this guide. In a 2022 Tipton County Chamber of Commerce forum, Underwood and Chris McNew (then the incumbent) answered questions on teacher retention and district programs [32].

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board president, running unopposed for the Cicero Township seat he first won unopposed in 2022 [6, 34, 31].
background: Elected to the Cicero Township seat in 2022 without opposition and joined the board in January 2023 [34].
Board president; re-elected to that post at the January 13, 2026 reorganization [31, 30].
path_to_ballot: Listed with the Republican label on the state candidate list; he is the only candidate for the seat [6].

items: As president he leads the board that approved the June 30, 2026 operating referendum resolution; no vote tally or individual statement was published in the coverage reviewed [37].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member. On the superintendent transition approved in 2025, he told the Kokomo Tribune, "I didn't want to do anything to disrupt that," referring to the year-long transition from Ryan Glaze to Scott Jaworski [28].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found.
gaps: No campaign website, occupation or campaign statement was found.
No 2022 candidate remarks were reported; he was unopposed and the 2022 forum article reported no remarks from him.

candidates.summary: Incumbent; elected to a City of Tipton seat in 2022 and seeking reelection [34, 30, 6].
background: Former teacher who taught at Southwood for five years before leaving the profession, and a relatively new Tipton resident as of 2022, according to the Kokomo Tribune [32].
Won one of two City of Tipton seats in 2022 with about 27 percent of the vote in a four-candidate field [34].
path_to_ballot: Listed with the Republican label on the state candidate list [6].

items: In 2022 he said the district should survey teachers, students and community members, including teachers who leave and families who choose other districts or choose Tipton [32].

Explaining his own departure from teaching in 2022, he said, "I think I left for the same reason a lot of people leave jobs, that is the culture and leadership," adding that pay was not the reason [32].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and serves on board advisory committees [30, 40]. No 2026 statement from him on the board's record, including the referendum, was found.

gaps: His positions are from the 2022 campaign; no 2026 statements were found.
